characters: Rahina: an inquisitive eight-year-old Ghanaian girl wearing a soft sky-blue headscarf and a neat yellow-and-blue patterned dress.
Ameyaw: her cheerful nine-year-old cousin with short hair, wearing an orange polo shirt and navy shorts.
Their mother: a warm Ghanaian woman in a blue-and-gold African-print wrapper cloth and headwrap, watching kindly from a carved wooden stool.

narrationPlan.voice: A quick, curious voice for Rahina; a cheerful voice for Ameyaw; calm for the mother
narrationPlan.pace: Curious and steady, building to the surprise (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A playful tune with water-drop sounds (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Many Ghanaian children live near rivers, lagoons, Lake Volta, or the sea, where wooden canoes are part of daily life. The story pairs a safe basin experiment with a clear rule about deep water.
Local fishing canoes, ferries, and life jackets make vivid classroom examples.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check that the explanation of floating (the boat pushes aside water, and the water pushes back up; the hollow shape holds air) suits Primary 1–2.
Check that the foil ball is squeezed tightly so no trapped air keeps it afloat.

teacherGuide.overview: A hands-on basin investigation showing that shape determines whether foil floats or sinks. Learners practise predicting, testing, counting load capacity, and following water-safety rules.
learningGoals: Sort tested objects into floaters and sinkers.
Explain simply why a hollow foil boat floats while a tight foil ball sinks.
State a clear safety rule for rivers and deep water.
beforeReading: Show five classroom objects and ask learners to predict which ones will float.
whileReading: Test one object at a time in a basin and compare with the class predictions.
afterReading: Fold small foil boats in groups and count how many pebbles each boat holds before sinking.
Draw a two-column picture chart of objects that floated and objects that sank.
discussion: Why did the same material sink as a tight ball yet float as a boat?
Why must every canoe or ferry respect its load limit?
reflection: What safety rules keep us safe near rivers, lagoons, or the sea?

mathsExtension.task: The foil boat carried 7 stones safely. Suppose a wider boat carries 3 more stones; how many stones is that in all?
Count the five tested items: cork, leaf, coin, stone, tight foil ball. How many sank?

support: Test three objects together and sort them onto two picture mats.
stretch: Design two foil boats with different floor widths and test which shape carries more pebbles.

culturalNotes: Many Ghanaian children live near rivers, lagoons, Lake Volta, or the sea, where wooden canoes are part of daily life. The story pairs a safe basin experiment with a clear rule about deep water.
Local fishing canoes, ferries, and life jackets make vivid classroom examples.
localiseThis: Connect the lesson to canoes and boats in your community.
Reinforce water safety: never go near deep water without a trusted adult and a life jacket.

factCheck.claim: A hollow foil boat floats even though the same foil squeezed into a tight ball sinks.
factCheck.explanation: Shaping the foil into a wide hollow hull encloses air and displaces more water, lowering overall average density so upward water push supports its weight.
